Speaking ahead of the 2026 Baden-Baden gathering, Leopoldo Camara, Head of P&C Reinsurance Northern, Central & Eastern Europe at Swiss Re outlined that more reinsurance capital is needed in the market to address growing, interconnected risks, while also emphasising that the reinsurer will use its deep risk expertise to align alternative capital where it makes sense.

“We see more capital flowing into the markets and into the reinsurance industry, and we think that is actually good news because more capital is needed to address the growing risks that we all need to deal with,” Camara explained.

Moreover, Camara underscored that different types of capital play different roles across the industry, highlighting the company’s long-standing commitment to reinsurance and its combination of capital with deep risk expertise.

“Our capital, the Swiss Re capital, is committed to the industry for a very long time. It is here to do multi-line reinsurance. So, we do life and health and P&C, we do short tail and long tail,” the executive said.

“The core business proposition of our capital, the core mandate is on the right side of the balance sheet. So, we’re here to play to pay claims. That’s our main promise: paying claims,” Camara continued.

“And we issue this promise, bringing alongside capital, deep risk expertise that we have acquired over more than 100 years. And this deep risk expertise, in our view, is absolutely indispensable to arrange risk transfer in a sustainable way, to help mitigate the risk, to actually measure and quantify the risk, to develop new risk transfer approaches, and also to align alternative capital when this makes sense.

“So, this is our kind of capital. That’s the kind of capital we’re bringing to Baden-Baden, and we actually see that our capital is in high demand.”

On the demand side, Camara noted that Swiss Re was seeing increasing amounts of systemic risk, with exposures becoming more interconnected and therefore more systemic.

The executive identified four key factors driving this trend: larger individual risks, intensified geographic clustering, enhanced integration of supply chain networks, and growing digital and social networks that amplify risk propagation.

“Larger individual risks, the prime example that comes to mind are data centers, where we see insured value concentrations in excess of billions, sometimes even tens of billions, in very small, limited locations. So, increasing amounts of large risk concentration,” Camara added.

Going back to alternative capital, Camara highlighted during the Q&A portion of the briefing, that Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in the space, through the use of its third-party capital markets focused Alternative Capital Partners (ACP) division.

“Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in a unit called Alternative Capital Partners. So we’re quite used and experienced in also deploying that kind of capital or supporting that kind of capital with what we bring to the table to enable alternative capital to actually take on risk,” the executive said.

At the 2026 Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous de Septembre (RVS) reinsurance industry event, Urs Baertschi, Chief Executive Officer, of P&C Reinsurance, underscored the importance of the reinsurers Alternative Capital Partners division, whilst also stating that Swiss Re expects to continue to be a “meaningful participant in that market.”

Liberty Mutual Reinsurance (LM Re), part of Liberty Mutual Insurance Group, has issued a parametric payout to the Mexican federal government for the 7.3 magnitude earthquake that struck Mexico’s southern coast in July, and activated Safehub’s Shake Network trigger.

The earthquake that struck Mexico’s southern coast on July 17th, 2026, triggered coverage under the government’s nationwide parametric earthquake and volcanic risk insurance program within weeks of the policy’s inception, for which LM Re has served as lead capacity provider of since June.

The federal program is overseen by Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, Mexico’s Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, and administered by Agroasemex, S.A., the Mexican state-owned insurance institution.

Moreover, the policy utilises ShakeNet Parametric, Liberty Mutual Re’s (LM Re) earthquake parametric insurance and risk management technology solution, powered by Safehub’s Shake Network and the Global Earthquake Model’s (GEM) OpenQuake engine.

By deploying Safehub’s propriety sensor network, the Shake Network reduces basis risk by bridging the gap between estimated models and actual ground motion.

Both companies confirmed that during the earthquake event, Safehub’s sensors recorded shaking within 80 km of the epicenter, delivering critical ground-truth to facilitate a precise and rapid trigger.

According to LM Re and Safehub, the Mexico program represents the largest ShakeNet Parametric deployment to date, backed by an extensive nationwide Safehub sensor network.

In addition, the parametric payment also meets Mexico’s government’s goal of ensuring fiscal resilience and continuity of public services after disasters.

As per the announcement, the deal was brokered by Augment Risk and domestic broker TBS.

Jean-Christophe Garaix, Head of Parametrics and Agriculture at LM Re, commented: “We are pleased to support the Mexican government in its disaster preparedness program. This claim payout reflects the effectiveness of how our solution can strengthen disaster resilience at a national scale, providing support when insureds need it most.

“It also showcases the growing demand for high-resolution earthquake impact data in risk transfer applications, with additional large-scale projects currently being developed in markets around the world.”

Andy Thompson, CEO of Safehub, said: “Ground-truth data is the key to aligning theoretical models with real-world impact and reducing basis risk. We are proud that Safehub’s sensor network and technology enabled a rapid, objective payout for the Government of Mexico. Earthquake resilience depends on actionable, high-resolution data and delivering that precision is at the core of our mission.”

In 2025, LM Re and Safehub launched a new earthquake parametric insurance solution that the pair at the time said will help reduce basis risk for parametric re/insurance policies.

Captives are rapidly evolving from risk retention vehicles into strategic capital access platforms, which in turn is beginning to attract third-party capital, according to broker Aon, who emphasises that captive owners are increasingly partnering with external investors to unlock capacity that supports growth initiatives and long-term resilience.

In a recent article, the broker underscores that captives today offer much more than an opportunity to reduce insurance costs and retain risk, noting that they are now being widely used to help businesses make strategic decisions around capital deployment and long-term resilience.

Aon also added that the evolving role of captives reflects a key challenge facing business leaders.

“Risks are changing faster than available insurance capacity. Losses from growing natural catastrophe, cyber and litigation exposures add pressure to balance sheets. In response, insurers are deploying capital more selectively, at times reducing line sizes and capacity. The resulting supply-demand imbalance has widened the gap between the risks organizations need to finance and the protection available through traditional markets,” the broker explained.

In addition, the broker highlighted that market leaders utilise captives to bridge this gap and strengthen their broader risk financing strategies.

Besides filling coverage gaps, captives also allow organisations to aggregate enterprise-wide exposures, access new sources of capital and unlock risk transfer solutions, such as insurance-linked securities (ILS).

Within a volatile risk environment, the broking group observed that key market participants are increasingly gravitating toward financing structures that deliver liquidity, expedited recovery capabilities, and enhanced predictability in the aftermath of loss occurrences.

In essence, captives function as a notable conduit to these mechanisms, enabling businesses to integrate parametric, reinsurance, and other alternative risk transfer methodologies into a single risk financing framework.

“The growth of ILS and other structured capital solutions is creating new ways to finance risk. Captives can help organizations access these sources of capital by serving as a bridge between enterprise exposures and investors willing to assume specific risks,” Aon explained.

The broker added: “Some of the most innovative captive strategies are beginning to attract third-party capital. Rather than relying exclusively on corporate capital, captive owners are partnering with external investors to unlock capacity that can support larger retention strategies, growth initiatives and resilience objectives.”

Aon concludes: “Captives are evolving from risk retention vehicles into capital access platforms, helping organizations connect exposures with the most efficient mix of traditional, alternative and third-party capital.”

Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, has placed an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion, noting there is the potential for the storm’s losses to add to aggregate structures.

Euler ILS Partners explained that there is a good deal of complexity in the loss assessment process, given much of the damage occurred from localised atmospheric turbulence.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall close to Destin, Florida early on Saturday morning local time, carrying Category 2 sustained winds of 105 mph and higher gusts.

As we reported at the time, market sources and reinsurance broker reports all pointed to pre-landfall estimates in the low to mid-single digit billions of dollars.

In a post-landfall report on the event we’ve seen, Euler ILS Partners explained and noted some complexity with the loss estimation process early after the hurricane, “We currently estimate insured losses at USD 2–4 billion. As is typical following a major hurricane landfall, uncertainty remains elevated in the initial post-event period, and industry loss estimates may be revised significantly as additional information becomes available.

“Loss assessment is particularly challenging because most damage resulted from complex, highly localised atmospheric turbulence. In addition, heavy rainfall across the Southeast before landfall contributed to large numbers of trees falling onto roofs over a wide area.”

The specialist ILS investment manager also stated, “Euler is actively monitoring the event and reviewing portfolio exposures. Current analysis indicates no impact on the portfolio. However, the insured losses may add to aggregate structures.”

Euler ILS Partners also explained that its analysis of the hurricane has been supported by the use of its recently launched Global Alert System, a tool developed in-house and in operation since June to provide “hurricane and typhoon forecasts up to 16 days ahead, earthquake and hurricane footprints at street-level resolution, and real-time alerts for earthquakes, tsunamis, wildfires, floods, volcanic eruptions and ash clouds.”

Other early loss estimates are now coming in for hurricane Isaias as well.

Accuweather said the expect the hurricane will result in an, “estimated $16-20 billion in total damage and economic loss across the Gulf and the eastern United States.”

Meanwhile, Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), has estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range, with the majority of losses expected to be located in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama.

While the industry has spent considerable time implementing ways that capital enters ILS vehicles, the mechanism for how it exits has often been treated as an afterthought. Artex Capital Solutions is dedicating effort towards building vehicles that provide a clear entry and a clear exit, with CEO Kathleen Faries emphasising that delivering clarity at the point of exit is essential to providing investors with full-lifecycle confidence.

Earlier this year, Artex Capital Solutions, the insurance-linked securities market service provider and insurance management specialist, partnered with legacy and run-off reinsurance specialist Enstar that introduced structured exit options embedded within Artex’s ILS vehicles.

As we explained at the time, this initiative was designed to solve the trapped capital issue for ILS investors, by providing mechanisms that can deliver greater certainty on exits from ILS investments, while providing liquidity and capital return.

Artemis spoke to Faries at this year’s Rendez-Vous de Septembre in Monte Carlo, who explained how this structure fundamentally changes liquidity expectations for ILS investors. The CEO also outlined whether Artex expects embedded finality to become standard across the market going forwards.

“I think that’s exactly what we’re aspiring to do. We’re looking to build infrastructure and structures that provide both a clear entry and a clear exit. Historically, we’ve relied on commutation language and collateral release provisions, but over time we’ve seen that those mechanisms may not provide the level of certainty some investors are looking for. This gives investors another option and greater confidence around the exit process,” Faries told Artemis.

She further explained: “We want to deliver efficient infrastructure from entry to exit, and the exit component is something Artex has been focused on building for some time.

“We manage many risk transfer vehicles globally including some that we own. The primary brand is Artex Axcell, which allows participants to rent a cell within our structure and access risk transfer efficiently.”

For investors, having Enstar’s exit and finality solutions embedded directly into Artex Capital Solutions managed and facilitated ILS structures is a meaningful step forwards towards making these features available and making trapped capital less of, or no longer a primary hurdle at all in future ILS investment structures they allocate capital to.

Furthermore, Faries also explained how amidst an influx of record-breaking catastrophe bond issuance, including a new record for first-half issuance at nearly $18 billion in H1 2026, how Artex is helping cat bond investors balance their search for yield with strict capital management.

“At Artex, we view ourselves as critical infrastructure for the market. That’s how I think about what we do as a company. Our role is to provide investors with efficient access to risk across the asset class and multiple ways to deploy capital,” the CEO said.

“That includes supporting catastrophe bonds, but also providing access to private transactions   across property cat, casualty, specialty risks, and parametric transactions. Artex has experience and infrastructure to support the full range of structures and lines of business in the market.”

Faries concludes: “Ultimately, Artex supports the market by creating efficient pathways for our risk transfer vehicles, capital to access risk in the way that best aligns with an investor’s objectives.”

While the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market stands as foundational source of reinsurance capital and continues to expand across various products, regions and perils, ILS Bermuda has highlighted the island’s central role in driving the global sector forward.

ILS Bermuda is comprised of leading professional organisations across the global insurance-linked securities sector. The group promotes economic development through the growth of ILS and alternative risk transfer in Bermuda.

ILS Bermuda is also the organising body behind Convergence, the annual ILS industry networking and education conference which takes place this week (Artemis will be in attendance).

“Bermuda remains a leading jurisdiction for the formation, regulation, administration and listing of ILS. Its established reinsurance market, specialist service providers, proportionate regulatory framework and capital-markets infrastructure support a broad range of structures and vehicles, including catastrophe bonds, special purpose insurers, collateralised reinsurance and sidecars, while also enabling emerging forms of risk transfer,” ILS Bermuda said.

The organisation also noted that the ILS market continues to heavily expand beyond peak U.S. natural catastrophe risk, highlighting that cat bond issuance and activity in recent years has extended into emerging perils such as wildfire, European flood and convective storm, cyber, casualty, sovereign disaster relief and other specialised risks.

This shift reflects growing momentum in the ILS market, as more companies have gained greater confidence in understanding the mechanics behind catastrophe bonds, sidecars, and other risk transfer structures.

Against this backdrop, Bermuda retains its position as the global hub for the ILS sector.

Supporting this, ILS Bermuda highlighted that the island registered 25 new Special Purpose Insurers (SPIs) and 10 new collateralised insurers during 2025, while also stressing that 2026 activity remains strong, with seven new SPIs and two new collateralised insurers registered in the opening quarter of the year.

In addition, the Bermuda Monetary Authority reports that Special Purpose Insurer approvals for catastrophe bond transactions are generally completed within three days, which helps support time-sensitive issuance.

Moreover, ILS Bermuda stated that the Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) represents an astonishing 95.4% of the outstanding 144A and private catastrophe bond market by value.

We recently reported, that the BSX has now listed in total 169 new catastrophe bond notes and insurance-linked securities structures in the first three-quarters of 2026, maintaining its global position as ILS listings leader and becoming home to the vast majority of listed ILS issuance so far this year.

ILS Bermuda further noted that a combination of parametric structures, enhanced modelling, cloud-based analytics and artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly expanding the ways in through risks can be measured structured and transferred.

“Investors continue to value the asset class for its potential to diversify exposure away from broader financial markets, while sponsors increasingly regard ILS as a durable complement to traditional reinsurance,” ILS Bermuda added.

“The market’s next phase of development is likely to be driven by disciplined underwriting, transparent structures, higher-quality data, deeper secondary-market liquidity and new applications designed to address global protection gaps.”

Concluding: “Bermuda plays a central role in the global insurance-linked securities market and continues to advance alternative risk transfer and reinsurance. Now in its 14th year, Convergence 2026 will bring together senior leaders, investors, asset managers, reinsurers, regulators, scientists and innovators for three days of focused discussion and relationship-building.”

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

As major hurricane Simon’s path shifted west it appears to have remained offshore of the important parametric trigger zones related to the $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bond, according to analysis by Isacco Loconte an insurance-linked securities (ILS) Investment Specialist at asset manager Azimut Switzerland SA.

As we had been reporting over the weekend, hurricane Simon’s minimum central pressure, a critical factor in determining whether any payout would come due for the catastrophe bond, did deepen to a sufficiently low level to activate a payout should the storm’s track have crossed into any of the parametric trigger boxes.

At one stage that was seeming increasingly likely to occur. But, again as we reported, it appeared that hurricane Simon had diverted away from the parametric zones just prior to breaching any of them and that no payout would come due in this case.

Analysis by Loconte suggests the same, as he has interpolated the hurricane’s path using the NHC data and found that while it was a very close call, hurricane Simon does not seem to have come close enough to activating the parametric trigger in this case.

“Based on preliminary NHC track data, the bond looks safe from a trigger event,” Loconte explained.

“Initial measurements indicate that Simon’s minimum central pressure (MSLP) entered the critical threshold for the bond (below 937 mb) at four track points between Oct 10 (18:00) and Oct 11 (12:00). While those pressure levels were strong enough to meet the L1 payout threshold for the parametric zones, the hurricane trajectory worked in the bond’s favor.”

Based on the parametric trigger design, hurricane Simon’s central pressure would have needed to be at 932mb or lower to activate a payout from the zones it came closest to. As we reported, at one stage the pressure deepened to 928mb as it approached the zone, but then the factor that drove the near-miss was the fact the storm’s track shifted slightly west and it moved parallel to the coast while a weakening trend began.

Loconte said, “As shown in the map below, the hurricane veered slightly west and remained offshore, avoiding direct landfall over the Jalisco region. Consequently, all four high-intensity points occurred at a safe distance outside the defined trigger zones.”

You can see Loconte’s analysis in the graphic below, showing the track veering to the west and away from the trigger zones.

You can see how close it came in the image above and had the storm continued on its original forecast path there was a strong chance Simon could have been very close to activating a 25% payout of the catastrophe bond’s principal.

Hurricane Simon is now set to make landfall further up the west coast of Mexico, but as the weakening trend has continued over night, there is now no risk of a trigger activation event occurring. The storm remains a danger to those on the coastline in the future landfall region, but having weakened the impacts should now be lower than if it had followed the original forecast path to hit Jalisco state head on.

Loconte explained, “Despite remaining forecast uncertainty over the coming hours (whether Simon turns further offshore or makes landfall further north in Mexico), the storm is expected to gradually lose intensity. As the storm weakens, its MSLP will move safely away from any bond trigger parameters.”

The Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) has now listed in total 169 new catastrophe bond notes and insurance-linked securities structures in the first three-quarters of 2026, maintaining its global position as ILS listings leader and becoming home to the vast majority of listed ILS issuance so far this year.

A heavy maturity load and some more early redemptions of mortgage insurance-linked notes resulted in the total value of ILS listings on the Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) falling through the third-quarter of 2026.

Having reached as high as $70.5 billion of ILS related listings on the exchange after the first-half of this year, the figure has declined slightly to almost $67.4 billion of cat bond and ILS listings on the BSX as of September 30th.

Naturally, issuance of new catastrophe bonds and ILS is slower in the third-quarter of the year.

Up to June 30th, the BSX had newly listed 146 ILS related securities and program structures, with a total value of almost $16.5 billion.

By the end of September, this had risen to 169 new listings of ILS securities and programs on the BSX in 2026, totalling nearly $17.8 billion.

As of September 30th 2026, the BSX was the listings home to 731 cat bond and related ILS listings, which amount to the $67.4 billion.

555 are related to catastrophe bonds, 552 of which cover catastrophic perils and 3 terrorism and financial guarantee risks. 166 listings from mortgage ILS deals and some cat bond preference shares make up the remainder.

Total catastrophe bond related listings on the BSX as of September 30th stood at almost $61.1 billion, down slightly from $62.6 billion at June 30th.

As of June 30th and based on our mid-year cat bond market outstanding record high of $65.6 billion, it meant the BSX accounted for 95.4% of the marketplace of 144A and private catastrophe bonds.

Now, a quarter later, after maturities and early redemptions that occurred, the BSX is still an impressive almost 93% of the total addressable market of catastrophe bond securities that could be listed as of September 30th 2026.

The Bermuda Stock Exchange continues to be the most important listing venue for the catastrophe bond and ILS market. We’d expect further growth and a potential new high to be set for the value of its ILS listings later this year, if the issuance pipeline proves to be as strong as market sources hope to see.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

Given most traditional alternative investments rely on the same economic drivers as the broader market, ILS highly differs because its returns are tied to natural catastrophe or insurance events rather than economic cycles, which leads Sage Advisory Services to say that investing in insurance-linked securities can achieve genuine diversification.

A new report, authored by Andrew Poreda, Vice President, Senior Research Analyst, explains that private credit, private equity, real estate, and infrastructure all offer different ways to access economic and corporate risk.

However, he points out that insurance-linked securities offer investors access to a different risk premium entirely, “across a $144.5 billion market in which catastrophe bonds are the visible half and privately negotiated reinsurance is the broader one, tested on a contract calendar that does not negotiate.”

“Most of what sits inside a typical alternatives allocation, whether private equity, private credit, real estate, or infrastructure, ultimately depends on the same small set of drivers. Corporate earnings. Financing costs. Refinancing availability. Exit valuations. Economic growth. These investments differ in structure and implementation. They do not always differ in what makes them work or fail,” Poreda explains.

“Insurance-linked securities, or ILS, are one of the few allocations that genuinely do. Their returns are driven primarily by insured catastrophe events rather than by the business cycle. For portfolios that have spent a decade adding alternatives without adding independent risk drivers, ILS is the missing piece.”

Further into the report, the VP emphasises that private equity depends on corporate earnings growth and exit markets, while private credit depends on borrower cash flows and refinancing, and real estate and infrastructure depend on financing costs, demand, and asset values.

Given this, each investment is highly sensitive to both the cost and overall availability of capital.

All of which leads Poreda to underscore how bringing ILS into a portfolio offers structural diversification and deterministic liquidity.

“A hurricane does not make landfall because earnings disappointed. An earthquake does not wait for refinancing markets to reopen. A wildfire is indifferent to the corporate default cycle. It also answers the realization question differently. A catastrophe bond matures on a date. The collateral is either returned or used to pay a claim, and the contract calendar decides which, not an exit market, a refinancing window, or a sponsor’s willingness to accept a mark. The valuation is tested at every maturity, whether or not anyone finds the answer convenient,” the report reads.

“The historical record reflects that independence. Sage research covering the most recent ten-year period found catastrophe bonds generated approximately 7.0% annualized returns with 4.6% volatility, a 1.53 Sharpe ratio, and a 2.50 Sortino ratio. Over the same period, cat bonds posted positive returns in roughly 79% of the months in which the S&P 500 declined.”

Importantly, the report also adds that the ILS market is not exempt from capital flows, going on to further explain that consistency within the space requires acknowledging that record cat bond issuance and strong inflows compress spreads in ILS as well.

The report acknowledges that cat bond spreads have tightened from their post-2022 peaks, whilst adding that recent index results have benefited from a period of limited insured losses rather than from structurally superior pricing.

“An investor allocating today should not assume the entry point that was available two or three years ago. The asymmetry is not that ILS escapes capital flows. It is what those flows do to the underlying strategy. In private credit, inflows create pressure to deploy. A manager who cannot source loans on the original terms chooses between holding capital idle and accepting something different, whether that means larger borrowers, thinner spreads, weaker covenants, or transactions outside the strategy investors funded. Fee structures and deployment expectations rarely reward patience,” Poreda continued.

Conversely he explains, “In ILS, a manager facing unattractive pricing can hold collateral, decline the renewal, and wait for the next cycle without changing the nature of the risk being underwritten. Catastrophe risk reprices on a regular renewal calendar rather than deal by deal, which gives capital a more visible mechanism for reflecting supply and demand.”

The report then turned attention to the private ILS market. Citing data from broker Aon, who estimates that total alternative capital deployed through ILS and related collateralized structures reached a record $144.5 billion as of June 30, 2026, Poreda also highlighted that outstanding catastrophe bond issuance reached a record $63.4 billion over the same period, up 17% year over year.

“That means catastrophe bonds represent roughly 44% of the ILS market. The remaining balance, on the order of $80 billion, sits in privately negotiated structures,” Poreda said.

Adding: “Aon describes the market as having matured into “foundational reinsurance capital,” and the composition reflects that. Outstanding sidecar capital reached approximately $23 billion across property and casualty lines, roughly 50% higher than year-end 2024, driven by growth in casualty-focused and asset-intensive structures. The balance sits in collateralized reinsurance, industry loss warranties, quota shares, and related private transactions.”

Given that private ILS contracts generally tend to be annual rather than multi-year, they resolve on a defined schedule rather than waiting on an exit market, and the loss determination turns on whether a covered event occurred rather than on a negotiated view of enterprise value.

Poreda emphasises that ILS remains considerably smaller than private credit, and capacity is finite. The VP observes that exposures can concentrate by peril, region, and season, and catastrophe modeling is an assumption-driven exercise that reasonable parties can dispute.

“ILS is a complement to an alternatives program, not a replacement for it. But the sizing question cuts both ways. A $144.5 billion market growing at 8.3% annually can absorb a meaningful allocation from a portfolio that currently holds none,” Poreda said.

“The practical case for ILS is not that it will out-earn private credit next year. It is that it does something the rest of the alternatives bucket cannot do for itself,” Poreda continued.

According to the VP, three key questions help to frame the sizing decision. What proportion of the alternatives allocation is contingent upon corporate earnings, financing costs or exit valuations? To what extent has the portfolio’s reported value been validated through external acquisition offers in recent periods? And what constitutes the source of capital, and what level of liquidity is genuinely necessary?

The report concludes by noting that alternatives allocations have expanded to represent one-third or greater of many institutional investment portfolios. Furthermore, more than nine in ten institutions currently maintain exposure to both major corporate-linked private exposures.

However, Poreda states that realization rates have decelerated throughout most asset categories, emphasising that valuations increasingly depend on estimates rather than market-based transactions, and liquidity has transitioned from a theoretical consideration to a practical operational constraint.

“Against that backdrop, the marginal alternatives dollar is worth more when it buys a different risk than when it buys more of the same one. Private credit, private equity, real estate, and infrastructure all offer different ways to access economic and corporate risk. Insurance-linked securities offer access to a different risk premium entirely, across a $144.5 billion market in which catastrophe bonds are the visible half and privately negotiated reinsurance is the broader one, tested on a contract calendar that does not negotiate. For portfolios that have spent a decade building the alternatives bucket, the next step is not making it larger. It is making it genuinely diversified,” Poreda concludes.

Pillar Capital Management, the Bermuda-based specialist collateralized reinsurance and insurance-linked securities investment fund manager, has secured a new high-profile backer as managing general underwriter SageSure has made a strategic investment in the company.

Pillar Capital Management is one of the leading managers of insurance-linked funds, having been founded in 2008. Today, one of its founding members Stephen Velotti is CEO and Chief Investment Officer of the company.

As of June 30th 2026, the ILS investment manager had around $4.3 billion of assets under management (AUM), placing it among the largest independent managers of ILS investment opportunities in the market.

Prior to this new transaction with SageSure, Pillar was jointly owned by its management team and global reinsurance company TransRe, a Berkshire Hathaway company.

With CEO and CIO Stephen Velotti and COO Tara Railton set to continue leading Pillar Capital, the announcement states that the firm’s management team will “continue to hold a substantial ownership stake in the business”.

We’ve learned that TransRe has now exited its stake in Pillar Capital, with SageSure stepping in as a key and supportive backer of the ILS manager.

SageSure is a specialist catastrophe-exposed property managing general underwriter (MGU) and well-known in the ILS market, for its forward-thinking approach to reinsurance capital and risk-sharing, having sponsored numerous catastrophe bonds under Gateway Re, while also sponsoring a number of reinsurance sidecar structures as well.

Now, SageSure has taken a strategic stake in a specialist ILS manager and with this comes alignment and access to capital, still from the ILS market and its investor base, as well as profit potential.

The MGU said that in acquiring a strategic investment stake in Pillar Capital, this “connects SageSure’s underwriting expertise with a broader range of capital sources across the property catastrophe value chain.”

Further explaining that the investment, “adds Pillar’s leading reinsurance risk underwriting capabilities and deep institutional investor relationships to the SageSure platform, expanding SageSure’s capabilities across the property catastrophe value chain and strengthening its ability to connect underwriting expertise with a broader range of capital sources.”

Pillar Capital will remain as an independent franchise, retaining its Bermuda-based team and investment strategy.

But now, this will be augmented by SageSure’s capabilities as well, in terms of risk-level insights, analytics and technology.

In addition, of course, this brings a new and closely-aligned route through which to access new reinsurance investment opportunities for Pillar Capital and its range of ILS fund strategies.

Pillar CEO and CIO Velotti commented, “We are excited to embark on this next chapter with SageSure. While our core strategy, our team, and the way we serve our investor partners will remain unchanged, partnership with SageSure will further enhance our ability to access, evaluate, and manage catastrophe risk and allow us to continue delivering industry-leading results.”

“For nearly two decades, Pillar has built a world-class platform and deep relationships with global institutional investors through a relentless focus on strong technical underwriting and prudent risk management, two principles which are core to our ethos at SageSure,” added Terrence McLean, President and CEO of SageSure. “For those reasons, I believe the two organizations could not be a better fit as partners.”

Howden Capital Markets & Advisory (HCMA) served as the exclusive financial advisor to SageSure on the transaction.

John Stamatis, Co-Head of North America, HCMA, stated, “This transaction is evidence of the growing convergence between traditional underwriting platforms and third-party capital. We have long had deep respect and admiration for both the SageSure and Pillar franchises, and are proud to have played a role in bringing them together.”

SageSure operates across 16 US states, with its insurance products currently protecting nearly 1 million policyholders, and the MGU manages more than $3 billion of inforce premium.

Pillar Capital Management is a multi-strategy ILS investment platform, dynamically allocating third-party institutional investor capital across reinsurance, retrocession, catastrophe bonds, and industry loss warranties (ILWs).

View information on many dedicated ILS fund managers, as well as reinsurers offering ILS style investment opportunities, in our Insurance-Linked Securities Investment Managers & Funds Directory.
